key_insight: This paper argues that effective ad-hoc teamwork needs agents to infer what a partner can actually do, rather than assuming partner skills are known in advance. By estimating partner capabilities, an agent can adapt to novel teammates and ambiguous, multi-strategy tasks more robustly.
problem_solved: Current ad-hoc teamwork methods typically assume a fixed task and pre-known partner capabilities. This work addresses the harder real-world setting where a partner's true abilities are hidden and human or AI teammates may choose suboptimal but valid actions.
method: Estimates a partner's action capabilities from observed behavior during collaboration.
Uses these capability estimates to adapt decisions in a task-agnostic way, instead of relying on a single predefined task model.
Supports teamwork with novel partners and settings where multiple valid strategies exist.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this improves robustness in human-AI and multi-agent systems where teammates are unfamiliar, imperfect, or unpredictable. It moves ad-hoc teamwork closer to realistic deployment conditions by reducing dependence on prior knowledge about a partner.
visual_elements: A before/after flow diagram showing traditional AHT assumptions vs. capability-estimation-based adaptation.
An observation-to-inference pipeline illustrating how partner actions are used to infer capabilities.
A multi-agent teamwork scene with hidden partner skill levels represented by icons or bars.
A comparison chart showing performance under known vs. unknown partner capabilities.
paper_title: Partner Capability Estimation for Task-Agnostic Adaptation in Ad-Hoc Teamwork
paper_authors: Peter Tisnikar, Maja Swieczkowska, Benteng Ma, Gerard Canal, Matteo Leonetti
